summary.text: The Renaissance was a European period and cultural movement at the end of the Late Middle Ages and the start of the early modern era.
It was marked by a revival of the literary, philosophical and artistic achievements of classical antiquity, and it began in Florence before spreading through Italy and Europe.
It brought great change in art, architecture and politics, with revolutions in printing and navigation and the arrival of modern banking and accounting.

facts.value: 15th and 16th centuries, or more broadly the 14th to the 17th

facts.label: Other major centers
facts.value: Venice, Genoa, Milan, Rome and Naples

facts.value: Phrase inspired by Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo

items.prompt: A scholar in the 1400s travels from monastery to monastery, hunting for forgotten Latin writings. What larger movement is this search feeding?

options.label: A campaign to replace Latin with everyday languages in every field of study
A plan to end the Church's role as a patron of art and learning
A revival of the literary, philosophical and artistic achievements of the ancient world
A project to translate only Greek and Arabic works on natural science

items.explain: Renaissance scholars like Poggio Bracciolini sought out ancient Latin texts as part of reviving classical antiquity. Studying Greek and Arabic natural science was the focus of the earlier 12th-century scholars.

items.prompt: Historians argue about how sharply the Renaissance cut off the era before it. Which view do many historians today favor?

options.label: That it was an extension of the Middle Ages, noting its medieval aspects
That it was a clean break from the past, focused on its early modern aspects
That it was only a short burst of art with no link to politics
That it simply repeated the 12th century with the same texts

items.explain: The traditional view stresses a break from the past, but many historians now focus on its medieval aspects and see an extension of the Middle Ages.

items.prompt: A historian traces the movement outward from its starting point. Which route matches how it spread?

options.label: Rome first, then Florence, and only later the other Italian cities
One Italian state first, then the rest of Italy, then throughout Europe
Spain first, then Italy, then the rest of Europe at once
Venice and Genoa together, with Florence joining much later

items.explain: It was first centered in the Republic of Florence, then spread to the rest of Italy and later throughout Europe.

items.prompt: A visitor in 1500 sees a grand painting of a religious scene that the Church paid for. What does this say about Renaissance humanists?

options.label: They turned away from faith entirely and avoided religious subjects
They worked only for private families, never for the Church
They copied medieval scholars and ignored ancient texts
Many of them did not reject Christianity, and many great works were devoted to it

items.explain: Humanists did not reject Christianity; many of the greatest works were devoted to it and the Church patronized Renaissance art.

items.prompt: Scholars in the 1100s translated Greek and Arabic works on natural science and math. What set Renaissance scholars apart from them?

options.label: A new focus on translating works of medicine and mathematics
A new focus on literary and historical texts of antiquity
A new rule that only Latin texts could be studied at all
A turn away from Greek writing in favor of Arabic works

items.explain: Renaissance scholars differed markedly from the earlier 12th-century scholars, who studied natural sciences, philosophy and mathematics rather than cultural texts.

items.prompt: Why did far more people gain access to books, the Bible included, as the Renaissance went on?

options.label: Rulers ordered every town to copy books by hand for free
Latin was banned from schools so everyone read the same tongue
Authors used everyday languages more, and the printing press arrived
Monastic libraries opened their shelves to the public

items.explain: Authors increasingly used vernacular languages, and combined with the printing press this allowed many more people access to books, especially the Bible.

beats.title: Looking Back to Leap Ahead
beats.hook: A movement that dug up the ancient past helped change how Europe made art, wrote about politics and handled money.

beats.prompt: A scholar in the 1400s wants fresh ideas about art, thought and politics. Where would a Renaissance humanist most likely look?
beats.explain: The Renaissance was characterized by the rediscovery and revival of the literary, philosophical and artistic achievements of classical antiquity.

choices.label: Back to the writings and art of ancient Greece and Rome
To the medieval Arabic works on natural science alone
choices.feedback: That was the focus of earlier 12th-century scholars, not what set the Renaissance apart.

choices.label: Only to brand-new inventions with no link to the past
choices.feedback: Inventions mattered, but the movement was characterized by reviving ancient achievements.

beats.prompt: Put these Renaissance moments in order.

items.label: First traces appear in Italy with Dante and Giotto
A resurgence of learning based on classical sources
Pico della Mirandola writes the Oration on the Dignity of Man
Charles V's assault on Rome ends the Italian Renaissance

beats.explain: Traces began in the late 13th century, the learning revival came in the 14th, Pico wrote in 1486, and the Italian Renaissance concluded in 1527.

right.label: Sought to describe political life as it really was
Led painters striving to portray the human form realistically
Credited with the 14th-century resurgence of learning

beats.explain: Each worked in a different field, from learning to painting to politics to philosophy, but all belong to the same movement.

paragraphs.heading: A rebirth of old ideas
paragraphs.text: The word Renaissance means "rebirth". It names a period and a cultural movement in Europe that came at the close of the Late Middle Ages and the start of the early modern era. Some date it to the 15th and 16th centuries, while others stretch it from the 14th century to the 17th. Its mark was a revival of the writing, thinking and art of classical antiquity, which Europeans rediscovered.

paragraphs.heading: Humanism at its core
paragraphs.text: The movement rested on humanism, an outlook built from the Roman idea of humanitas and from rediscovered Greek philosophy. Humanist scholars such as Poggio Bracciolini hunted through monastery libraries for ancient Latin texts. After Constantinople fell in 1453, Greek scholars fled west carrying precious manuscripts, many of them long forgotten in Western Europe. Humanists did not turn away from Christianity, and the Church paid for a great deal of Renaissance art.

paragraphs.heading: Starting in Florence
paragraphs.text: The Renaissance first took hold in Florence, one of many Italian states, and then spread across Italy and later Europe. Many trace its ideas to Florence around 1300, in the writing of Dante and Petrarch and the painting of Giotto. Explanations for why it began there point to the city's politics, the patronage of its leading family, the Medici, and the arrival of Greek scholars. Venice, Genoa, Milan, Rome and Naples became other major centers.

paragraphs.heading: New ways of seeing and writing
paragraphs.text: In art, Florentine painters led by Masaccio tried to show the human body realistically and found ways to render depth and light more naturally. Linear perspective was one of several techniques for painting a more natural-looking reality. Authors also turned more and more to vernacular languages, alongside Latin and Greek. Together with the printing press, this put books, above all the Bible, in the hands of far more people.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond the arts
paragraphs.text: The changes reached well past painting. Machiavelli and other political thinkers set out to describe politics as it actually worked. The era helped shape the customs of diplomacy, and it saw revolutions in printing and navigation along with the arrival of modern banking and accounting. Thinkers like Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo, skilled in many fields, gave us the phrase "Renaissance man".

paragraphs.heading: A spark in 1401
paragraphs.text: Some writers give the Renaissance a precise birthday. In 1401 two rival artists, Lorenzo Ghiberti and Filippo Brunelleschi, competed to make the bronze doors of the Baptistery of Florence Cathedral, and Ghiberti won. Others see a broader contest among Brunelleschi, Ghiberti, Donatello and Masaccio for commissions as what sparked the creativity.

paragraphs.heading: Was it really a break
paragraphs.text: Historians still argue about what the Renaissance was. The older view treats it as a clean break from the past. Many historians now stress how much it carried on from the Middle Ages, and some question whether the label is useful at all. Panofsky described the two eras as linked "by a thousand ties".
